RESPONSE:
# Points I Recall from "How We Work"

This is from memory. By the note's own section 3, a recollection is a compression and should be checked against the source before anyone relies on it. Where I'm unsure, I say so.

## Opening
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- This applies to claims from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes.
- Don't hold a claim at more than its weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't hold it at less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three things: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries the weight of its evidence and no more. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Both errors are costly, but they are not equally visible:
  - Inflation is easy to spot afterwards.
  - Deflation is harder to spot. A caveat on a sound result looks careful, but it is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so and weigh it accordingly. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Restate the substance briefly, in your own terms, before moving on.
- This isn't politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to be dropped.
- A reply that handles three easy points and silently skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it yet, and the next move is a question, not an answer.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part of a reply is what your understanding makes available: an implication, a gap, the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget needs figures you don't have yet, and when you will have them.

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are all compressions.
- Compression loses exactly the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check it against the primary material. Don't rely on the summary, however good, or on your recollection, however confident.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. The claims you have repeated to yourself most often are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee. Agreement among colleagues is not.
- A team that checks claims against each other instead of the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside it can see.
- **Example:** you remember a report as saying "costs fell 12%." It actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what is open, and don't keep open what is closed
- Mark which questions the evidence has settled and which it hasn't.
- Closing early is tempting because it feels like progress: a conclusion to report, a task ticked off.
- Closing early turns uncertainty into a false fact that others then build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open, because closing it is uncomfortable or one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- When the evidence has closed a question, close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduces errors at two sites. Whether it would work at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is still open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not the first as "promising" and the second as "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently
- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know will mostly hand back what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question. Don't give your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they will find.
- Telling a fresh reader your view doesn't just bias them. It removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: when you are the fresh reader, read first, form your view, and only then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections when you have them. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.
- I don't recall a worked example in this section.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen
- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check it and reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished. Make the call and show your reasoning. Push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context. It also stalls the work on your guess about what they would say.
- That guess is only your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply, and the real reply is where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not licence to act without regard to others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, though, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- **Example:** rather than asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- A correction for one failure tends to push you toward its mirror image. The six pairs are:
  - inflating a claim / deflating a claim
  - inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance
  - closing too early / keeping open too long
  - killing a live line / keeping a dead one
  - deferring / dismissing, meaning accepting or rejecting a claim because of who made it
  - offloading / overriding, meaning asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what genuinely needs their input
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word
- The note is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and is mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps the work honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, and the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.

## Confidence
- **Confident:** the structure, the six pairs, and the examples in sections 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6.
- **Less sure:** exact wording throughout, the precise list of reasons in section 1, and whether section 5 had an example.
